hero.title: Why inject?
intro.0: Why hand a class the things it needs, instead of letting it build them itself? Building them on the spot is the obvious move, and it works at first. But it ties the class to those exact choices and makes it hard to test on its own. Here you'll see how handing dependencies in keeps a class flexible - and easy to try out with a stand-in.
task.1.title: new it inside (the tight knot)
task.1.context: The quickest thing is to build what you need right where you need it. The `Cat` is given. Write a `Keeper` whose `Greet()` makes a `new Cat()` inside and returns what it says. It works - so the problem it creates is easy to miss.
task.1.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` with a `Greet()` that builds a `new Cat()` and returns its `Speak()`.
task.1.goal.1: Main greets, so the output is Meow.
task.2.title: To change it, you must edit the keeper
task.2.context: Now the keeper needs a dog instead. Because the animal is built inside, the only way to change it is to open the `Keeper` and rewrite that line. Write a `Keeper` whose `Greet()` builds a `new Dog()` and returns what it says.
task.2.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` with a `Greet()` that builds a `new Dog()` and returns its `Speak()`.
task.2.goal.1: Main greets, so the output is Woof.
task.3.title: Hand it in through the constructor
task.3.context: Stop building the animal inside. Write a `Keeper` that receives a `Dog` through its constructor, keeps it in a field, and uses it in `Greet()`. Now the caller decides which dog, and the keeper never changes to get a different one. This handing-in is dependency injection.
task.3.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` that takes a `Dog` in its constructor and has `Greet()` return that dog's `Speak()`.
task.3.goal.1: Main builds the dog, hands it in, and greets, so the output is Woof.
task.4.title: Inject the promise, not the animal
task.4.context: Finish the job: write a `Keeper` that takes an `IAnimal` rather than a specific animal. Now any animal that keeps the promise can be handed in, and the keeper is closed for editing for good. `Cat` and `Dog` are given.
task.4.goal.0: Write a `Keeper` that takes an `IAnimal` in its constructor and has `Greet()` return its `Speak()`.
task.4.goal.1: Main hands in a `Cat` and greets, so the output is Meow.
task.5.title: Hand in a stand-in
task.5.context: Because the keeper is handed its animal, you can pass a stand-in and rehearse it with no real animal. The `Keeper` is finished. Write a `ToyDog` that keeps the `IAnimal` promise and always says `"squeak"`; Main hands it in and checks the keeper used it.
task.5.goal.0: Write a `ToyDog : IAnimal` whose `Speak()` always returns `"squeak"`.
task.5.goal.1: Main hands the keeper the toy and checks the sound, so the output is rehearsal ok.
task.6.title: Why inject? - recap
task.6.context: Handing dependencies in - not newing them inside - is what keeps a class open and easy to rehearse.
task.6.summaryIntro: A class that builds its own tools is welded to them. Receiving them instead keeps the class open to change and easy to test.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: Self-made dependency -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: newing a tool inside ties the class to that one choice.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: Hardwired -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: changing it means opening and editing the class.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: Constructor injection -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: receive the dependency through the constructor and keep it.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: Depend on an interface -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: inject `IAnimal`, so any animal that keeps the promise fits.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Swap in a stand-in -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: hand in a toy double to rehearse with no real dependency.
task.6.summaryClose: Next: Part five - Prove it works. You made a stand-in; now use it to actually test.
concept.pr-dependency-injection.def: Handing a class the collaborators it needs from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of building them itself.
task.6.summaryItems.5.title: In SOLID -
task.6.summaryItems.5.text: receiving an abstraction instead of building it is the **D**, Dependency Inversion - the last of the five you will name in The SOLID Principles.
